title: The seed dispersal design lab
subtitle: Use structures and a fair model to explain a journey
objective: Explain how seed or fruit structures can aid dispersal and evaluate a controlled paper model.

sow.alignment: New investigation outcome; dispersal models do not demonstrate evolutionary adaptation by need. Original secondary-age exemplar at an upper-KS2 conceptual level; no qualification approval or completion claim.

priorLearning: Know that seeds contain an embryo and can develop into plants.
Read repeated measurements in a table.
success: Link a structure to a dispersal mechanism.
Identify what changes and what stays the same in a model test.
Use repeat data without claiming measured outdoor dispersal distance.

vocabulary.meaning: Movement of seeds away from where they formed.
A flowering-plant structure that develops from the ovary and contains seeds.
The shape and arrangement of a part.
A simplified representation used to explore an idea.
A condition kept the same for a comparison.

equipment: Shared seed/fruit cards and constructed test results, selected route, pencils; optional calculator.
Optional adult-only demonstration: two equal 4 × 16 cm paper strips; one folded into a compact shape, one with a simple rotor shape; metre rule and clear drop area.
preparation: Default lesson uses the complete constructed dataset. Label any optional observations separately.
For a rotor: slit the top half lengthways into two equal blades; fold them in opposite directions. Fold the lower half into a narrow body. Keep all paper attached so mass is retained.
Use equal paper stock and original dimensions for both models; do not add clips or change the release height.
safety: No climbing, throwing or blowing seeds. If demonstrating, an adult releases models from a marked reachable height above a clear floor.
Use pre-cut paper where needed; no real berries, hooks or seeds are handled or tasted.
practicalAlternative: Use the supplied model design and constructed fall times. Pupils can investigate all decisions on paper without making or dropping anything.

misconceptions.claim: A wing means the seed flies using its own power.
misconceptions.correction: Wind-dispersed structures interact with moving air; they do not choose or power a journey.
misconceptions.check: Ask what moves the air or object.

misconceptions.claim: Longer fall time proves a longer real outdoor journey.
misconceptions.correction: It can give wind more time to act, but actual distance also depends on wind, height and other conditions.

misconceptions.claim: The plant grew a wing because it wanted to move.
misconceptions.correction: Useful inherited structures exist through evolutionary processes, not an individual plant’s intention.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether a seed makes a decision.

access.supported: Match structure and mechanism; compare one pair of fall times.
access.standard: Analyse repeats and explain controls and limitations.
access.stretch: Calculate means and redesign a distance test while separating model from organism.
access.regulation: Offer private writing, pointing, drawing or adult scribing. Allow pass-and-return for public questions and desk-based participation. Choose support from current learning evidence, not fixed ability labels.

slides.title: A seed has no engine
body: How could a seed travel away from its parent?
Look for a structure and a force or carrier.
slides.notes: Invite a structure-based guess. Avoid intention language such as the seed wants to fly.

slides.title: Seed, fruit and a fair comparison
body: R1. What can a seed develop into?
R2. Where are seeds found in a flowering plant’s fruit?
R3. Why repeat a measurement?
slides.notes: A new plant in suitable conditions; inside or associated with fruit structures depending on species, accept within fruit for core model; repeats reveal variation and strengthen confidence.

slides.title: I connect structure to a journey
body: A sycamore wing interacts with air.
A burdock hook can attach to fur.
The transported object can include fruit around a seed.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I name the structure before the mechanism. A wing supports interaction with air, not self-powered flight. Hooks support attachment, not growth towards an animal. Diagrams are selective.

slides.title: I design a fair paper comparison
body: Change the paper shape.
Keep mass, release height and method the same.
Measure fall time, not imagined travel distance.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Explain exact retained paper and optional rotor instructions from preparation. The constructed test uses no added clip. A clear drop avoids disturbance; pupils may remain entirely on paper.

slides.title: I keep the claim within the measurement
body: A longer descent gives air more time to act.
We measured seconds to the floor.
We did not measure real seeds outdoors.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Think aloud: I cannot turn a fall-time result into a kilometre claim. This is a limited model of structure affecting descent, not proof of every dispersal outcome.

slides.title: Model design jury
body: W1. Match A–C to wind or animal dispersal.
W2. Compare the repeated fall times.
Which shape stayed in the air longer here?
slides.notes: A wind; B external animal attachment; C animal ingestion. Rotor times exceed compact in every paired trial; use a pair such as 1.4 vs 0.8 seconds.

table.caption: Constructed sample data only; no outdoor distance was measured.

slides.title: Detect a broken comparison
body: A team changes shape and adds a heavy clip.
Can it attribute the difference only to shape?
Name the repair.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. No; mass also changed. Use the same retained paper mass and no extra clip, with matched release conditions.

slides.title: Choose the honest caption
body: W3. Repair “The rotor proves sycamore seeds always travel farther”.
State the measured result and one limit.
slides.notes: The rotor paper model took longer to fall in this setup; actual seed distance depends on wind, structure and environment. Model does not establish all-species ranking.
slides.reveal: In this paper test, the rotor fell more slowly. Real dispersal distance was not measured.

slides.title: Which quantity was measured?
body: Choose the conclusion that fits the test.
slides.notes: A is correct: the measured quantity is fall time. B is false: no outdoor distance was measured. C is false: the structure did not change intentionally.

options.text: The time each paper model took to reach the floor.
options.feedback: The units are seconds and the release conditions are stated.

options.text: How far every real seed travels outside.
options.feedback: The test used paper models indoors and did not measure distance.

options.text: How much the seeds wanted to move.
options.feedback: Wanting is not a scientific variable for a seed.

slides.title: Your independent investigation
body: Choose one response route.
Explain a structure and evaluate the model evidence.
Use numerical values and a clear limitation.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across the three You do slides. Supply shared page 1 and one selected route page. All routes target the stated science objective; a labelled drawing or independent dictated explanation is valid.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Name what changed and what stayed the same.
Keep seconds attached to fall-time values.
Do not claim a measured distance.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Ask pupils which evidence supports their explanation. Read prompts or scribe without supplying the scientific conclusion.

slides.title: Check before sharing
body: Does my explanation answer the question?
Have I named the evidence or process?
Have I kept the conclusion within its limits?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Use the route-specific worked answers to identify one precise next step.

slides.title: Compare and improve
body: Show one structure–mechanism link.
Check a numerical comparison.
Improve one claim about real seed journeys.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Offer partner or private teacher feedback. Ask for one specific revision linked to evidence; no public ranking.

slides.title: A question worth investigating
body: Suggest one next question about this lesson’s evidence.
Choose a question whose answer would improve our model.
slides.notes: Lundy cycle: invite written, spoken or pointed suggestions. Select one feasible question and explain how the pupil contribution changes the next example or investigation.

slides.title: Show the science you can explain
body: E1. Explain how a wing can aid dispersal.
E2. Give evidence from the paper model.
E3. Give one limit of this model.
slides.notes: The wing interacts with air and slows descent. Accept an accurate pair of fall times. This paper model measures indoor fall time, not outdoor dispersal distance. E4 asks for one control.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: dispersal jury
pupilPages.intro: All fall times below are constructed sample data, not class observations.

cards.title: A • Sycamore
cards.text: A seed is enclosed in the base of a winged fruit. The wing can slow descent and help wind carry it.

cards.title: B • Burdock
cards.text: Hooked burrs can attach to animal fur and be carried away before falling off.

cards.title: C • Fleshy fruit
cards.text: Some animals eat fruit, digest the flesh and later pass surviving seeds elsewhere. Survival is not guaranteed.

cards.title: D • Test method
cards.text: Constructed test: same paper stock and original 4 × 16 cm size, all paper retained; same 1.5 m release height and rule, still indoor air. Shape changes. Fall time is measured.

blocks.prompt: W1. Match A–C to a dispersal mechanism. W2. Compare one pair of times.
W3. Improve the “always travels farther” claim and name a limit.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: structure and evidence
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Point, circle or explain with a short sentence.

blocks.prompt: S1. A sycamore wing mainly helps interaction with …
S2. Burdock hooks can help attachment to …
S3. Complete: In trial 1, rotor paper took ____ s and compact paper took ____ s. The ____ stayed in the air longer.
S4. Name one condition kept the same in the paper test.
S5. Does this prove real outdoor travel distance? Explain.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: design jury report
pupilPages.intro: Use the shared evidence and state exactly what was measured.

blocks.prompt: N1. Explain a wing, hook and fleshy-fruit dispersal route.
N2. Compare the two models using two pairs of times and units.
N3. Name the changed variable, two controls and the measured quantity.
N4. Explain why adding a clip to one model weakens a shape-only comparison.
N5. Give a bounded conclusion and one model limitation.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: design a stronger test
pupilPages.intro: Do not confuse fall time with distance.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate the mean fall time for each paper shape and compare them. Show working.
T2. Explain why the model supports a possible role for a wing but cannot prove every real seed travels farther.
T3. Design a later model test of horizontal distance using controlled airflow. Name the change, two controls, repeated measurement and units.
T4. Evaluate “plants grew hooks because they wanted animals to carry them”. Write a scientific replacement without intention.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Use evidence and an honest limit.

blocks.prompt: E1. Explain one structure–dispersal link.
E2. Compare two fall times from page 1 using units.
E3. What does the paper model not establish?
E4. Name a control and explain its purpose.
Reflection. What should the next model measure?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: New plant under suitable conditions; seeds are associated with fruit structures, core example inside fruit; repeats show variation and support a more reliable comparison.

answers.label: W1–W3 / design fault
answers.answer: A wind; B external animal attachment; C animal ingestion. Rotor exceeds compact in all trial pairs: 1.4/0.8, 1.5/0.9, 1.3/0.7 seconds. Adding a clip changes mass as well as shape; match mass. W3 bounded paper fall-time conclusion, not all real seed distances.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A correct. B no distance measured. C intention is not the measured variable.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: Air; animal fur; 1.4, 0.8, rotor; any stated control; no, paper indoor descent time is not an outdoor distance measurement.

answers.label: N1–N5
answers.answer: Wing interacts with air/slows descent; hook attaches to fur; animals can ingest fruit and later pass surviving seeds. N2 correct paired values/units. N3 shape changes; mass, release height/rule and airflow controlled; time to floor measured. N4 added mass is another changed factor. N5 rotor took longer in this setup; limits include paper structure, indoor still air and no distance measurement.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 compact (0.8+0.9+0.7)/3=0.8 s; rotor (1.4+1.5+1.3)/3=1.4 s; difference 0.6 s. T2 longer descent may allow more wind influence, but actual distance depends on many conditions. T3 vary one shape under fixed airflow setting, release height and model mass; repeat and measure horizontal landing distance in cm. It is a planning task, not an instruction to improvise a fan practical now. T4 useful inherited structures can aid dispersal; individuals do not develop them because they want a ride. Evolutionary detail is optional.

answers.label: E1–E4 / assessment
answers.answer: Correct structure–mechanism link; accurate pair and seconds; not real outdoor distance; relevant control/purpose. Secure: mechanism, fair variable distinction, numerical result and limit. Re-teach overclaim by underlining seconds and asking what was actually measured. Reflection accepts a precise next variable or measurement.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.
The default investigation is fully paper-based. Any optional adult demonstration is a separate observation, labelled as such; it must not overwrite the constructed sample record.
A sycamore dispersal unit is a winged fruit containing a seed; burdock burrs carry fruits/seeds. Keep the seed-versus-fruit distinction accurate without overloading the supported route.
Interactive decisions use the same structures, test conditions and times as W1–W3.
